records.text:
pstack v0.15.27 ships with a new skill /create-formal-verification-skill! 

it's still in beta, and similar to /create-verification-skill, this is a meta-skill that creates a new skill and formal verification suite based on the characteristics you want to verify. for example, you may want to model state machines and systems with concurrency using TLA+, or use kani in rust to check for undefined behavior. 

if you're new to formal verification, think of it as mathematically proving properties and invariants (something that must always be true) or "laws" of your system. usually, this means modeling your programs in a separate language like with TLA+ and then running the solver on that spec. newer approaches like with kani and @bendlang take a different approach where there is no separate language: you write kani in rust, and bend in bend (it's also a programming language, and the proofs are written as laws and expressed in its type system).

historically formal verification never reached mainstream status because of the difficulty in modeling and writing proofs. it's quite difficult to model your business requirements and keep them in sync! but i expect that we will see more innovation in formal verification in the future as being able to formally verifiy that the code does what you intended gives your agents superpowers in writing correct software.

in the meantime though, i've been experimenting with modeling our code with TLA+ and have already found several bugs with the skill created by /create-formal-verification-skill. 

try it out and let me know how it goes!

records.text:
these results are really interesting! i can see two sides forming: one that sees agents as an extension of their own mind - like a cyborg, and the other that sees a future version of them as independent artificial beings, capable of making their own decisions and working alongside us.

with that framing, i can see why ~70% of people said no: they imagine a future where you have brain computer interfaces that remove the need to type words into an input box. there may come a time where it no longer feels like you're chatting with another entity, agents augment you in a way that feels like an intuitive system 1 extension of your body, removing the barrier between thought and action. 

i can see the argument for why chat might be final too: just think about how we collaborate with our colleagues, friends, and family: we just talk to them. you don't need anything else. i think voice chat and text chat are actually the same thing in this sense. in this category you see an agent as more of an "other", it's own entity, rather than a part of you.

which side are you on? or are you somewhere in the middle?

quotedPost.author: KentonVarda
quotedPost.text:
Prediction: Most people will stop using docs, slides, or spreadsheets in the next year, instead prompting an agent for custom code for every task.

Each of these apps is just as "easy mode" version of something else that used to take far more time and skill to create:

Docs: Easy mode web site.
Slides: Easy mode video / animation.
Spreadsheets: Easy mode custom app + database.

But now you can just prompt an agent to build the "hard mode" version for you and they are damned good at it.

(Note: I'm not suggesting that humans shouldn't write. You can still write text, and then ask an agent to turn it into a web site that supplements your text with diagrams, animations, hierarchical organization, etc.)

quotedPost.author: TimSweeneyEpic
quotedPost.text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

What's more of a surprise is the emergence of AI as a sort of insta-Carmack able to solve hard technical problems quite cleverly and often cleanly, and that it's able to reason about and work in complex 3D scenes both by operating the tools and by directly understanding the raw data files.

I abandoned assembly language in 1998 when out-of-order CPUs made much simpler C/C++ code faster, and never I missed it. If prompting through architectural documents, concept art, and design plans can transcend typing code and tweaking vertices, that will enable developers to spend their time on higher-level, higher value technical and creative tasks.

What matters is the end product, whether it's a game or an engine. Anything developers can do to try out more ideas and make better software and games faster is a win for everyone.

records.text:
Harness durability in https://t.co/OL0LzGtvAw.

The same 𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎𝙵𝚡𝙰𝚐𝚎𝚗𝚝() is now *durable* on your laptop or in the cloud, via files, Postgres, or Vercel Workflows. Node.js or Bun.

Agents need long-running compute. But they also need to tolerate restarts, redeploys, timeouts, crashes…

Concretely, if a user sends a prompt and then throws their phone into a black hole, we ensure that turn runs to completion. If the process crashes mid-tool-call, it resumes from there.

To this end, 𝚕𝚒𝚋𝚏𝚡 introduces a simple durability adapter API. On Vercel, it leverages all the infra we built for durable workflows and queues, giving you reliability with 1LOC.

This is a critical aspect of production-grade agents (and something all @eve agents also get out of the box). Next, we'll show you how we bring the same durability to Pi, OpenCode, and even your own custom harnesses.

records.author: poteto
records.text:
how do you trust your agents' work more? copy this post/link and give it to your @bot or agent!

1. codebase improvements: this is just good software engineering - better architecture, stronger types and invariants, clear boundaries. agents love to copy what exists and take the shortest path, so make the easy thing the right thing. categorically eliminate problems through code and you won't need to think about it again.
2. static analysis: lint rules, tests, CI, verification (eg TLA+). very token efficient ways to catch issues ahead of time.
3. prose: comments, rules, AGENTS.md, skills - anything that can't be enforced and requires agent judgment. use it minimally, but do use /create-verification-skill.
4. human review: the hardest to scale. at the rate agents land code, it's pretty much impossible to thoroughly review every PR, so spend that effort on the highest leverage point, designing an environment where agents do the right thing by default.

this forms an inverse pyramid: you want most of your effort at the top, least at the bottom. codebase improvements are deterministic, making it more token efficient, and lets you sleep more soundly at night.

install https://t.co/u9xIlN3eN0 and create a new Project:
1. look through my slack/chat messages and code review comments where i've given feedback on PRs, code, architecture
2. use /recall on my past transcripts to learn how i steer agents
3. /poteto-mode use /correct and /architect on past commits to find the most common pitfalls agents fall into, then propose a plan to rearchitect the code i own so it's more agent friendly. answer open questions with prototyping rather than defer to me, and back the plan with real data. 
4. before you begin, use /sharpen + /in-your-own-words and confirm this prompt with me

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
recommended reading. i like the term "coherence" over "taste".

historically, simplified, a human would approach a software writing human, asking them to build a thing. that's an iterative process, until software writing human truely understands what the other human needs and wants. which is also why we moved away from waterfall. you often can't know what you want before you've build a first shitty solution you can feel out. and your wants might change.

in this scenario, the outcome is what matters, not the program structure itself, unless that makes the outcome worse/impossible (bugs, perf, ease of adding features). 

the software writing human's skill is not so much programming itself, but understanding the other humans wants, pulling out domain knowledge from the other human, asking questions, and ultimately translating the other human's wants into programs, while ensuring the program structure is fit to be modified for future needs.

now, can you replace the software writing human with an agent? for simple one-off stuff, yes. if the human with a want is technically minded that extends to more complex programs. 

most humans suuuuuck at this iterative colab with agents tho, as they are bad at structuring and communicating their wants. 

and agents currently still suck at the software writing human skill of colaborating with another human to understand their wants and translate them to a program.

my gut tells me that this is because the training data and RL for coding agent tasks is largely composed of trajectories where a software writing human and an agent colaborate. that missed the other half of the problem: the human with a want and software writing human interaction.

and until we can encode that agents for writing programs will likely only be effective in the hands of software writing humans, or very technically minded humans.

another thing agents currently suck ar is translating software writing human shallow instructions into architecture that's not a house of cards. i think this too is a consequence of the lack of training data/RL-able trajectories that encode the process a team of software writing humans go through when building a thing. we do have digitized artifacts (design docs, commits/PRs, issue trackers) that capture some but not all of that.

i think this will improve, as we all are now doing design sessions with our agents, so labs could in theory train on that. however, even if this data were available and becomes part of training, the pretraining data still has tons of shit code from around the internet in it, ehich posttraining would have to combat.

welcome to my morning word salad.

records.text:
comments are unstructured and unenforceable text. agents do read them but they are often ignored, go out of date, and gives your agent an escape hatch to do a bandaid, hack or a workaround instead. 

use this prompt to audit your code comments to find opportunities to improve your code through stronger types, better API design, and create lint rules so the comments aren’t necessary!

https://t.co/pl1siCHE8i

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
ban and delete most if not all code comments!

agents love copying what already exists. a seemingly harmless comment explaining some temporary workaround is one of the worst viruses you can have in your codebase. like a weed it'll spread quickly as a tool for agents to quickly get their job done. before you know it, your codebase is overrun with hacks and stale comments. just one more workaround bro 

you can use pstack's /no-comments skill as a weedkiller. it'll seek out useless comments while keeping the ones that actually should exist (like explaining a browser quirk), and figure out how to solve them on a first principles basis

here's a prompt you can try asking @bot:

create a project agent that uses /poteto-mode to spawn a /swarm to use /no-comments and identify useless code comments we can prune in my repo. come back with a high level plan of which of these workarounds would be best solved by refactoring and which we can straight up delete

https://t.co/nqeRdY62ee

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
it's easy to fall into the trap of micromanaging your agents instead of correcting the environment that shapes its behavior. 

pstack 0.15.9 now ships a new /correct skill: if you keep correcting agents for the same mistakes, it finds the pattern and fixes it with architecture, types, and checks.

i like to imagine that commits rapidly flowing into the codebase are like a bonsai tree rapidly growing in whatever direction it pleases. what you want to do is not to give in to the chaos, but tame it intentionally with the right constraints

0.15.9 also has improvements to:
• /architect: now includes instructions on designing agent friendly architecture
• a new /benchmark-checklist skill based on @brendangregg's benchmarking checklist

here's a prompt you can give to grok bot to start architecting a better codebase with pstack: 

/poteto-mode create a new Project agent to refactor and rearchitect my repo so that our architecture is more agent friendly. it should use both the /correct and /architect skill to look through past commits and find the most common pitfalls that agents fall into, whether its with code quality, performance, or bugs. if relevant you can also use the /recall skill to find past conversations for context. it should make a high level plan for me to review. it should also answer its own open questions by prototyping rather than defer to me. come back to me with a plan backed by real data. once i approve the plan, use either the stack or full autopilot playbook (ask me which i want) to execute

records.author: rauchg
records.text:
This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment.

When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company.

There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome.

Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today.

I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet.

Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

records.text:
perhaps one of the most durable parts of pstack are its engineering principles: very concise skills (~10-20 loc) that distill down good practices into its core. 

as models get smarter, i expect most of pstack skills to compress into short principles or workflows (a generic list of steps) and that i will be able to delete a few of them. 

how it works is that /poteto-mode contains a short index of available principles and tells agents "In your reply, name each principle that shaped a decision and the specific choice it changed." this is why you'll often see a Principles Named or Used section at the end of the agent's response

many of these principles were extracted from my sessions correcting agents since the start of this year. some are inspired by problems i see people talk about, like Attack the Premise, inspired by @VictorTaelin's post https://t.co/qTGVfoKSyD

you can also use the principles as skills if you want greater control, by invoking /principle-<name> 

https://t.co/wuTWsflVN3

quotedPost.author: 0xkydo
quotedPost.text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

These are precisely the types of code we should refactor and improve now that we have extremely capable agents. Action at a distance in particular is a big footgun for humans and agents alike, why wouldn’t you want to remove it if you can? 

The reality is also that the comments agents write are anything but good. What you’re saying makes sense when humans still wrote all the code, but agents do now

records.author: poteto
records.text:
• comments go stale very quickly and confuse agents and people
• they are often used by agents to explain workarounds that would've been better off actually fixing the code instead
• they are not enforceable and waste your agents' tokens

my point is that moving prose (comments, rules, agent.md, skills) into deterministic lint rules, better API design/types, is far more effective, enforceable, and token efficient.

comments are simply a crutch that agents will happily misuse

i don't think that software will die, but i predict that it will look very different. existing "legacy" software will get consumed into the chat box and effectively become tool calls.

but i also think whole new kinds of software, many of which we haven't even seen yet, will be created. i wrote about this before but i think that as the barriers to entry for coding fade away, a new generation of developers will invent a whole new meta for building software and it will like totally unlike anything we've seen before

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
on a related note, there's been some chatter recently about software engineering skills (eg the ruby/rust/elixir drama). i'm a bit torn because while i do feel like they're software engineering principles and patterns are still important, at the same time i wonder if there will come a point in time when they just won't matter anymore. not that they're no longer useful, but that your own intuition can fill in the gaps as you use agents in an intuitive sense rather than knowing explicitly what they're doing

if that doesn't make sense, the analogy i have is the first iphone. 20 years ago you had to be a professional with expensive equipment, now just with a phone and some creativity you can film content that's compelling to a new audience. i don't know if there's a term for this but i want to call it "skill compression". where what used to be gatekept and prohibitive to experts becomes accessible to a new audience of creators with a whole new meta. the details have sort of faded away and now the craft is not in knowing the equipment and how to use it, but how you use it creatively

we're going to see a whole new generation of builders who've never seen or written a line of code build incredible things

records.author: poteto
records.text:
i love writing. i never let agents write for me. whether it's docs, or tweets, or shitposts, or even prompts (okay maybe that one's harder as agents manage other agents) 

there's a simple reason for that: i still strongly believe that writing is thinking. it's a skill i hope to never give up. it's also important to me that whatever i say is always authentic, mistakes and all. my favorite posts are the ones that i just full send without any editing

i suspect it also helps with prompting. being able to clearly express what i want, and knowing the vocabulary i need to be able to direct my agents does seem to make for more effective usage of agents. in the same way that engineers have an advantage when we prompt agents to write code, because we are intimately familiar with the words that make up the discipline

knowing the right word incantations to get an agent to produce a desired goal almost feels like spellcasting. as models get more capable, and that input box looks more and more like a magic box that can output anything, words become the interface between you and the genie

there may come a time when we give up the keyboard in exchange for brain-computer interfaces. but until then, i'm writing every word.

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
something that keeps bothering me is how some people see slop as something that is happening to them, like they're some kind of helpless bystander powerless to do anything about it

excuse me but you are a software engineer, you literally learned how to make sand think and make computers do your bidding?! and now you can't do anything about it? please

the 2 things you should know to cut through all the noise:

1. you need to give your agent a way to verify its own work (i just posted about this so won't rehash)
2. your codebase is memory

the 2nd is not new either, we have always had lint rules, compilers with good diagnostics and strong type systems, LSPs, etc to help us write better code. there is no difference when agents write the code instead, you just need more of them, and stronger ones.

forget rules and skills. you can add those later.

yes, your codebase is a form of memory to agents! agents love extending what already exists. so every nit and every annoyance you've ever seen, every mistake and bad pattern you observe from agents, needs to turn into a constraint, or the agents will just keep repeating those same mistakes like a virus in your code. then you keep observing and repeating this process until your codebase is locked down enough that even agents with little context can one shot a high quality PR.

an even better direction is to refactor/rewrite your code such that agent anti-patterns become categorically impossible. use type systems to your advantage, use libraries/frameworks that reduce the architectural search space, or heck, create your own framework like we did for grok bot and design high quality primitives and well thought out APIs

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
agentnis goven tools, e.g. read, write, edit, bash. two call them it makes tool calls, e.g.

user: do the rhing
assistant: ok, [read(...)]
read result
assistant: ok next [bash(...)]
etc.

each of these is a turn, i.e. an llm request plus tool execution.

with code mode, the llm gets a tool where it writes a little program, in which all the other tools (read/write/edit/bash) are available as functions.

it can then process many more things in a single turn by writing a program that does many tool calls instead of calling tools directly.

saves turns, and let's the llm filter / transform stuff depending on its needs.

records.author: poteto
records.text:
okay now that we're past that tired discussion, let's talk about how we get agents to write more correct code (note: this won't mean the code will be Good, but it should at least work)

this is the entrypoint into your most basic agentic loop: verification. it means giving your agent the ability to verify its own work, most commonly by actually running and interacting with it like a real user would. whether your interface is a cli/api/ui/whatever, you want to start here so that your agents can close the loop. if you want you can even have your agents model the problem in TLA+ and attempt to verify if you have things like state machine bugs.

the point is to give yourself confidence in the agents' work by them producing some kind of artifact that proves that 1) that the work is correct, 2) that it matches what you intended, and 3) is easier to review than reading the whole PR. most commonly this would be a video and/or screenshots for UI work.

everything else like skill packs are really bonus and optional, all you need is a way for your agents to verify their own work to start using them more autonomously. some caveats are that not all domains can be verified easily yet, and that verification is just approximation and can still be wrong. it's no different than trusting that a human actually ran the code they wrote and trusting it

so start here!

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
pstack now includes 2 skills i recommend everyone use or copy:

/create-verification-skill
https://t.co/xYQArsuVWR

/maintain-verification-skill
https://t.co/J5s8WL1itT

if you don't already have one, /create-verification-skill creates a skill that teaches your agent how to run, control, and debug your app.

it also creates something i call the feature map: a map of all the features in your app and how to get to it and use it from a user's pov. it allows agents to navigate and use the app just like a real user which greatly increases its ability to verify its own work. but of course, this feature map goes out of date very quickly.

run /maintain-verification-skill as a daily automation with cursor cloud agents. this skill will check your app for changes and keep your feature map up to date.

having a strong verification skill will end up becoming critical infra for your team and become the foundation of boosting everyone's productivity and quality and also enable more interesting automations to be built.

install https://t.co/WDB4U1rwmu and you'll get auto updates for my skills. enjoy!

quotedPost.author: thorstenball
quotedPost.text:
There's some senior engineers on here who, in the face of AI changing the very structures this industry is built on, present themselves as Stewards of the Craft of Programming.

Bugs the hell out for me.

They keep alluding to the virtue of doing things by hand, the value of Good Code and of craftsmanship, saying that yes, AI might change some things, but hey it won't ever change the value of something done with proper care, by hand, just like in the olden days of 2024. Most everything that was Good back then is still Good now: deep knowledge of languages and systems, good code, great architecture. You know the sermon.

And, yes, some of that *is* true. At least I think so. But we don't know, because no one truly knows what will be important in the future.

We're going through times of great change and I think the best advice to give to young people and others who want to have a job and provide value is: keep your eyes open, rethink from first principles, derive from what businesses value what you can provide; the digital world is more malleable than ever, you should rethink how you can help shape it.

All this pounding on the Bible of Good Code seems to me to be doing the opposite: it lets people feel comfortable -- what I've valued all my life is still valuable, I can rest easy -- in times when one shouldn't feel comfortable. This is a bumpy, exciting, strange ride. If you lean back you might fall off the waggon.

Let's not delude ourselves and others that we can keep doing what we've been doing. Rethink it all.

And, like I said, it bugs the hell out of me seeing senior engineers (that are secure in their career) talking as if there's nothing *really* to change, because the Fundamentals will still be valued. They might!

But it's the wrong advice to not rethink everything right now.

records.text:
it's very interesting how many replies i've gotten about maintainability and clean code being still important. i would argue that that is no longer true and we all need to update our priors on what Good Code really means in 2026.

clean code has always come at a cost - performance. indirection and making code readable/understandable for a human is not free, it often comes at the cost of worse performance. we have historically been okay with this because of Moore's Law and the fact that most code is not on the hot path. 

these principles also came from a time where humans maintained code. it made sense to optimize for humans then, but it makes less sense now when agents are already writing all the code. we will in fact probably discover and come up with new principles: principles of agent friendly architecture (i plan to write more thoughts about this soon)

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

i actually intentionally left out maintainability/complexity as properties of good code. not that I don’t think they’re relevant, but they’re properties of the syntax not properties of the output, which are the 3 I landed on. it’s also weird for me to say this (as i do take care with my agents to write maintainable code), but my hypothesis is that it was only good because humans wrote the code. the real goal with those best practices was to make “code easy to change” (by humans). 

well, agents, especially those running on the latest frontier models, can work in any codebase. code is easy to change! you can simply refactor and rewrite code trivially by just telling it to. therefore the only properties that matter are the runtime aspects: correctness, bug free, fast and efficient

put another way: when agents write everything, does it matter if the code is concise or clean if the other 3 properties are true?

records.author: poteto
records.text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

quotedPost.author: patrickc
quotedPost.text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

quotedPost.text:
Pi 也将要Rust重构？Mario 刚在 X 转发 Prime Intellect 用 Rust 重写自身推文时，顺手调侃了句「pi goes rust. it just cost a few tokens」，底下有人问是不是愚人节，他特意回了一句「猜猜旧 TypeScript 代码库是基于什么写的」

这表面调侃下游烧了两千亿 token，但让人联想到 pi 官方是不是也在盘算把底层迁到 Rust 上

其实社区早就按捺不住了。此前 Dicklesworthstone 就做过获得 Mario 许可的纯 Rust 移植版 `pi_agent_rust`，把并发全切到了 asupersync；社区里还有个叫 pie 的 Rust 重构分支。大家自己动手的诉求很直接：甩掉 Node 运行时、单二进制分发、大幅压缩启动延迟和内存占用

这次 Prime Intellect 调动 2000 多个 Agent 搞自主重构，同样是因为并发瓶颈。在上万个并发沙盒集群里调度多智能体，TypeScript 的进程底噪和资源开销会被成倍放大

越来越多的终端 Agent 底座都在往 Rust 靠拢。如果把核心 Harness 和流式调度交给 Rust，把 TypeScript 只留给动态插件与扩展，或许正是 pi 下一步最合理的解法

on a related note, there's been some chatter recently about software engineering skills (eg the ruby/rust/elixir drama). i'm a bit torn because while i do feel like they're software engineering principles and patterns are still important, at the same time i wonder if there will come a point in time when they just won't matter anymore. not that they're no longer useful, but that your own intuition can fill in the gaps as you use agents in an intuitive sense rather than knowing explicitly what they're doing

if that doesn't make sense, the analogy i have is the first iphone. 20 years ago you had to be a professional with expensive equipment, now just with a phone and some creativity you can film content that's compelling to a new audience. i don't know if there's a term for this but i want to call it "skill compression". where what used to be gatekept and prohibitive to experts becomes accessible to a new audience of creators with a whole new meta. the details have sort of faded away and now the craft is not in knowing the equipment and how to use it, but how you use it creatively

we're going to see a whole new generation of builders who've never seen or written a line of code build incredible things

quotedPost.author: matth_lapeyre
quotedPost.text:
We did not know how long Microduck would actually last on battery 

We had thermal management issues with our Radxa prototypes: throttling after just 20 minutes, followed by an overheating shutdown.

We addressed this with the new custom board. To test it, we let Microduck roam autonomously in a dedicated area, walking around, standing and sitting until the battery ran out.

The results are way better than we hoped :)
- Over 3 hours on a 2600 mAh battery. 
- Estimated average battery current dropped from ~1.13 A to ~0.82 A, roughly 28% less.
- Peak CPU temperature dropped from 114°C to 60°C, with zero thermal throttling throughout the test.

This time, the battery ran out before the cooling did :)

Very happy with the progress!

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were an engineer before agents came along, you're rightfully skeptical about lines of code and number of PRs being used as a metric for any kind of productivity. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective as being an engineer on a large team of at least 50. 

volume didn't matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few PRs: for example you could make a one line config change and save the company millions of dollars.  

but before agents, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who is struggling to perform, on the other end you might have someone who was a "coding machine" archetype. a coding machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room and emerge with a stack of PRs that solve a huge number of problems. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you've ever worked at a large tech company before, you'll get what i mean. the thing about agents is that big tech co problems are now small-medium co problems as well. 

how do agents change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a coding machine. you have incredibly capable frontier models that can write code better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you're still producing the same number of PRs as before, why wouldn't you pause to wonder why you're not being more productive? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can't outship a human coding machine?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust (https://t.co/7fzYZV8LGH). if you haven't put in the work to trust your agent's output, it is very difficult to scale up your productivity. 

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before agents, this cost was very high - you needed to hire many software engineers with high 6 figure salaries to do the work. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time (https://t.co/gTBZx7pl14) factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 moths to a year. a single engineer with agents can do the work of tens if not hundreds of engineers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don't think has hit yet is that job of the software engineer has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce software any longer (well tbh it was never only about the code, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the software. this idea of a software factory, or a Michelin kitchen as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it's the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what's possible when you put a lot of rigor into using agents at scale

records.author: rauchg
records.text:
One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum.

There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

quotedPost.author: NathanFlurry
quotedPost.text:
we upgraded to pi-durable for rivet actors!

~~~

if curious what the hype is all about:

agents are a disturbed systems problem, and one that’s easy to do wrong

there are ~so~ many edge cases when something fails at any step of the loop, including:
- process crashes & ooms
- upgrading your code
- retrying tool failures
- resuming partial turn completion
- prompt retry exactly once delivery
- llm providers go down
- network timeouts
- failure to write durable state
- and subagents are a different beast

all of this needs to be handled or else background agents will behave erratically

pi-durable does this for you

it takes learnings from workflow engines and building a harness + tools that handle resuming, history, and idempto-, erm, i-dem-poten-cy, erm, idemp-o-tency beautifully

highly recommend listening to mario & armin yap about durable (link below)

~~~

rivet actors then give you a way to orchestrate pi durable:
- global singleton process for each pi instance
- each pi instance takes 1.3 mb of ram
- starts in ms
- sleeps when idle
- works with or without a sandbox

durable also works seamlessly with actor’s sqlite, crons, workflows, otel, jwt, and other goodies we’ve been crafting

and open source of course

quotedPost.author: mitchellh
quotedPost.text:
I've published a new, general-purpose terminal specification that gives any program a way to tell the terminal what it's doing: idle, working, waiting, finished, or failed, and why. It is easy to implement on both sides. I've written more about why: https://t.co/2FfzNC3F8T

The problem this solves is generic and applies in compelling ways to all sorts of use cases (e.g. package managers, build tools), but it really rears a hideous head when it comes to AI and the "agentic inbox" problem.

I found over 250 different agent orchestrators (with various goals) that all individually implement a heuristic based approach to detecting whether things like Claude Code are working, blocked, done, etc. 

If you look at @herdrdev's commit history, you can see around 10 compatibility changes to detect Claude Code within just the past 3 months. (This isn't a dig at Herdr! They're doing great work with what they have, and everyone else is doing the same thing). 

Heuristics are not the way. And over-indexing on agentic use cases isn't the way, because this problem is really interesting for other tools too: Homebrew, Terraform, Cargo, etc. etc. 

Proprietary protocols and out of band APIs are not the way. They have an O(N) integration problem and require extra work to work over SSH or within local VMs/containers.

The program status specification (OSC 7501) solves this in a reliable, deterministic way that is general-purpose and can be easily adopted by the entire industry. 

Read more: https://t.co/2FfzNC3F8T

records.author: poteto
records.text:
something I have been thinking about is a way to approximate how well you’ve setup your codebase for agents. think of it as a thought experiment and rough heuristic, not a real number that can be compared

it’s not a fully formed idea yet, but i think there’s something to the idea of “time to (fully automated, hands off) rewrite” or ttr

as a thought experiment, lets say you decided to rewrite your code in a different language/framework/architecture. how long would it take a single engineer to do it?
 
the number itself isn’t that important, but it leads you to more questions that can help you directionally figure out how to make your codebase more legible and productive for agents. 

for example, maybe you think your ttr is high because you wouldn’t trust the final result - because your agents don’t have a way to verify their work and convince you that their output is identical in user visible behavior to the original. well, that inability is likely also a problem today and slows you and your agents down 

there’s also a more subtle question of the quality of the rewrite that would be produced. is perf better, the same, or regressed? is the code easy to delete and extend? and how much do you trust the rewritten version to be able to maintain its quality over time as PRs start flowing into it?

what do you think?

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
ship a new agent version (new prompt, new tool, changed state) and reopen old conversations.

tardigrade replays the log since its last snapshot through the new code. if that part contains model calls made with the old prompt or tools, the thread won't open. snapshots holding the old state shape fail too. 4 of 12 cases pass.

classic event sourcing tradeoff, temporal solves it with explicit versioning in code.

pi durable never replays history through code. the next turn uses the new prompt and tools, documents carry a version and a migrate function.

(12 cases for tardigrade vs 6 for pi durable. tardigrades outcome also depends on whether a snapshot exists, so we test both. pi durable has no snapshots.)

this one's from our own harness benchmark, outside of durable objects (also in the repo, see link at end of thread)

the interesting bit for me is the middle chart. in tardigrade a single write gets more expensive the longer the conversation gets, because each commit re-derives state. agents write a lot: every message, every tool call, every status update.

in pi durable a write is a write, no matter how long the conversation.

i think this too could be fixed in tardigrade to have constant cost.

records.author: thsottiaux

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
one tradeoff tardigrade makes due to its event sourcing design is memory, at least in the current implementation.

an open thread keeps its entire derived state in memory. at 3000 turns that's 83 MB of heap vs 34 MB for pi durable, and the gap grows with history.

that could be fixed with persistent projections that are cheap to read. which is basically what pi durable does. i'm sure june already has ideas for that.

pi's memory usage also grows, but is capped by the model's contrxt size.

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
tardigrade and pi durable both try to solve durable agent execution: an agent can crash and pick up where it left off. different designs for the same problem, each with its own tradeoffs.

tardigrade derives everything from one event log. pi durable stores the transcript as plain records, plus small documents with their own operation logs (much smaller than the transcript, and optionally without history).

i think pi durable is the better design for what we need to evolve pi and build new products. but tardigrade is excellent and very well thought out!

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
as i said, june's benchmark actually surfaced an issue in pi durable at this somewhat unrealistic history size. the fix was pretty small. the numbers below are before and after. all other numbers in this thread are with the fix.

i also fixed up the benchmark harness and replaced june's DO adapter for pi durable with a built in one that doesn't copy every row.

thanks, june! super helpful, never thought of that being a possible issue.

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
digging into it a little, cold and warm turn timings for each history size.

tardigrade is event sourced. it keeps a log and snapshots its state every 500 events by default. a cold start reads the last snapshot plus the events after it, reduces and validates them. that snapshot is the entire conversation history, every message plus every model request and tool result, potentially far more than fits into the llm's context. once loaded, all of that stays in memory. we'll come back to that.

pi durable just reads the part of the conversation that goes into the llm context (everything since the last compaction; here compaction is off, so all of it), with no state to rebuild or validate. 

3500 turns is ~11.7k messages, ~250k tokens here because the benchmark's tool results are tiny (256 bytes). that fits a 1M token model, but a real coding agent with real tool output would have compacted many times over by then. still, a benchmark is a benchmark :)

records.author: bcherny
records.text:
I am surprised that people are surprised this is how I prompt Claude.

Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker. There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks -- give Claude a goal, and it will figure it out.

Back in the Sonnet 3.5 days, your prompt mattered a lot. Nowadays, it's much more important to communicate to the model:

1. What you want it to do
2. How much effort you want it to spend
3. How it should verify that it did the right thing

records.text:
i just automated our release and QA process!
using Grok Bot i made two Team Bots: sandcastle, my release manager, and poteto, my engineer bot. i added them to Slack and made a new channel for managing releases.

first i tell sandcastle that i want to do a cut. it'll DM all the contributors with links to their PRs so they know what goes in the next release and can DM the bot back if they have any blockers or objections.

sandcastle then kicks off the build, watches it automatically, and starts up an automated fuzz swarm. usually this is 10+ agents running on Grok 4.7 xhigh to run the build, click around and use it like a real user (using our verification skills and feature map), some are directed while a few are "chaos monkey" clicking things randomly to see what breaks. 

whenever it finds an issue, i tell it to @ mention my engineer bot poteto, to spin up a Cursor Project to own triaging and fixing all the high pri issues. depending on the severity i may ask it to cherry pick the fix into our release branch and cut a patch release, or if it's a pre-existing issue i still fix it but include in the next release instead

that's one more tedious task that Grok Bot now handles for our team

records.author: poteto
records.text:
my favorite use case for Grok Bot is for the first and the last mile of getting work done.

the first mile is figuring out what work you should even be doing at all. that involves connecting Bot to the different apps and services you use, so that it can grab whatever context it needs - whether it's your calendar, your CRM, slack, email, or the many other connectors available. then, the first mile begins when you combine these connections, allowing you to provide context to your bot ("look at this slack channel for new features we've built and then look through our CRM to see which  customers we should nudge") instead of micromanage it.

you can automate further by setting up routines - they let your bot do something on a schedule ("check my email every morning") or as a reaction to something ("do this whenever this slack channel has a new message"). so a new lead can kick off a whole workflow that you setup for your bot, allowing you to delegate the work you would otherwise have to do to your bot!

the last mile involves actually following through and closing the loop. one example of this is building a new feature, or fixing a bug that your customers have reported. this is where Bot can hand off tasks to Cursor - our engineering focused agents that can write code in the cloud, on their own computers.

when you've gotten the hang of this, the next thing you can try is building a loop. here's a simple example that i use daily:

1. watch this slack channel for feedback about our app
2. create a ticket for this in Linear
3. create a Cursor cloud agent to triage and reproduce the issue on its own computer, using pstack
4. if the issue clearly reproduces, put up a fix and fuzz the pull request with a small swarm of agents
5. if the fuzz has no issues, ping me on Slack, and rebase and auto-merge the PR after 1 hour unless i request changes

you can also install my bot Dr Eggbot and ask it to teach you how to setup a loop like this for yourself!

https://t.co/U1shj39y3J

records.author: thsottiaux
records.text:
Day 2.1/

We have made Auto-review free for all users signed in through a ChatGPT account. You can enable it in settings > permissions > auto-review. Auto-review improves upon the default sandbox setting that requires you to approve everything, which is prone to decision fatigue unless you spend a lot of time configuring specific rules.

It allows you to run long tasks while having a second agent review all actions taken by the primary agent. Its only goal is to prevent high-risk actions from being taken and to protect against unwanted actions that are not aligned with the original user intent. This  Auto-review feature is now free and does not draw usage from your plan.

records.author: rauchg
records.text:
Introducing gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript.

gdp-ts is a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require 'proofs' that the caller performed an authorization check.

The typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing your team and agents from shipping catastrophic security (and other kinds of) bugs.

While these patterns have existed for quite some time, especially in ecosystems like Haskell, ① human code review and ② cognitive and syntactic overhead made these solutions niche.

The situation is now inverted. Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they *thrive* in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all.

The README and examples model a real-world Vercel API product constraint: changing the password on a Project requires a proof of a certain role + a certain entitlement. Thanks to Matt Noonan and Ollie Charles for their research in this space.

https://t.co/eRWdiMvQ2V

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
effect/workflow is kinda close, but it uses the temporal durability model with memos + replay to reestablish the call graph. that makes code changes + migration harder.

in our model you have versioned tasks, that define migrations themselves. then on resume, the task scheduler checks all pending tasks, migrates them if needed, and carries on executing thrm. this also allows you to swap out task implementations in process without close/resume.

unsure what an effect version of this could look like.

records.author: badlogicgames
records.text:
we provide primitives to durably commit state in tasks and tools. these can then themselvey become durable using those primitives.

e.g. say you add a "subagent" tool. each tool invocation has a unique id, so you first check if you already created a subagent for that subagent tool invocation specifically via that unique id.

if this is a replay, you get the previously saved state, e.g. the subagent id, and the id of the request you send to it.

if this is a fresh call, you create the subagent convo and submit the request and store the subagent id and request id.

then, for both cases, you just join on the request id until you get the data.

quotedPost.text:
everything i know about managing agents i learned from the amazing programmers and computer scientists that came before

constraints in your codebase are freeing for both humans and agents! this has always been true, but if you were a small dev team you likely never had to think that deeply because you could trust your fellow programmers to write code and review well

but large companies have had to solve this problem since even before agents. because before you had agent slop, you had human slop. lots of engineers wrote bad code out of necessity (eg backend engineer forced to write frontend or reverse). the solution to this was constraints: lint rules, smarter compilers and diagnostics, high quality tests, investments into observability, and so on

the arrival of agents just means that big company problems are now everyone's problems. the good news is that none of this is really that novel: it's just good engineering

Go is a great language and runtime that has served us wonderfully @vercel to build large-scale, resilient infrastructure.

Highlights & some realtime figures:
▪ Our global TLS stack (50K TLS handshakes per second)
▪ Our build outputs cache is serving 250K RPS right now
▪ In-region static asset cache is serving 128Gbps

We recently overhauled our DDoS and WAF stack in Go:
▪ Evaluating 600K events per second with new stream processing system
▪ Issuing 10K actions (blocks / challenges / shadow tests) per minute
▪ 8.5X faster mitigations than legacy version (and 40x faster at peak), industry-leading performance

Go has helped us serve the biggest election in terms of Internet traffic of our times and https://t.co/lOZVWvVnLs without breaking a sweat.

Another highlight is that Go hits a sweet spot of having bindings available for both low-level kernel and systems calls, as well as a very successful ecosystem of cloud APIs and SDKs. Modern infrastructure work involves a combination of both types of work. Go was instrumental in enabling our new compute platform powered by Firecracker (https://t.co/nptrqIIdCz) and our ability to improve compute density and cost-efficiency with In-function Concurrency (https://t.co/SMsZh9WaxB).

If you’re interested in systems-level programming, especially in Go or Rust, my DMs are open. It’s an amazing time to join us to build the tools and infrastructure for the next billion developers.

quotedPost.text:
everything i know about managing agents i learned from the amazing programmers and computer scientists that came before

constraints in your codebase are freeing for both humans and agents! this has always been true, but if you were a small dev team you likely never had to think that deeply because you could trust your fellow programmers to write code and review well

but large companies have had to solve this problem since even before agents. because before you had agent slop, you had human slop. lots of engineers wrote bad code out of necessity (eg backend engineer forced to write frontend or reverse). the solution to this was constraints: lint rules, smarter compilers and diagnostics, high quality tests, investments into observability, and so on

the arrival of agents just means that big company problems are now everyone's problems. the good news is that none of this is really that novel: it's just good engineering

https://t.co/ykgu52qBqB

records.author: rauchg
records.text:
DHH is fundamentally right about Rust. For context, Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification (carcinization, technically 🦀) for a while.

One of the first projects we migrated was Turborepo, from Go to Rust¹. The migration completed, but the RoI was actually quite controversial internally.

While Rust was in our eyes better for low-level OS access, something crucial for a build system like Turbo, the human migration costs were very sustantive.

Go is very fast. It's beautifully designed. It's easy to iterate on. We were very conflicted about the migration, because it was *humans* writing the code, *even if we knew Rust was a better choice*.

The calculus has now changed. What's "best for humans" is no longer necessarily "best for business". 

FWIW, it's also quite unlikely that Rust is the end-all-be-all toolchain. I'm quite certain there's greener pasture ahead, because Rust itself was designed before the 'supersonic tsunami' of agents hit.

¹ https​://vercel.com/blog/how-turborepo-is-porting-from-go-to-rust

records.author: poteto
records.text:
it's easy to fall into the trap of micromanaging your agents instead of correcting the environment that shapes its behavior. 

pstack 0.15.9 now ships a new /correct skill: if you keep correcting agents for the same mistakes, it finds the pattern and fixes it with architecture, types, and checks.

i like to imagine that commits rapidly flowing into the codebase are like a bonsai tree rapidly growing in whatever direction it pleases. what you want to do is not to give in to the chaos, but tame it intentionally with the right constraints

0.15.9 also has improvements to:
• /architect: now includes instructions on designing agent friendly architecture
• a new /benchmark-checklist skill based on @brendangregg's benchmarking checklist

here's a prompt you can give to grok bot to start architecting a better codebase with pstack: 

/poteto-mode create a new Project agent to refactor and rearchitect my repo so that our architecture is more agent friendly. it should use both the /correct and /architect skill to look through past commits and find the most common pitfalls that agents fall into, whether its with code quality, performance, or bugs. if relevant you can also use the /recall skill to find past conversations for context. it should make a high level plan for me to review. it should also answer its own open questions by prototyping rather than defer to me. come back to me with a plan backed by real data. once i approve the plan, use either the stack or full autopilot playbook (ask me which i want) to execute

quotedPost.author: poteto
quotedPost.text:
every time you intervene and correct your agent, you should think about how to eliminate it entirely. 

in order of value:
1. categorically eliminate the problem through better architecture or choice of data structures
2. turn it into a lint rule or test so CI catches it
3. turn it into a skill or rule
4. have humans review the code to catch it (ngmi)

records.text:
Security will become a larger and larger function in software companies. Security is verification engineering (eg: “my code is probably memory-safe”), as well as capital allocation (“what surface should I throw most tokens at?”)

For startups, it’s a challenge and opportunity. As the world’s paranoia grows given ever-more-sophisticated AI adversaries, how can you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company?

But conversely, given the dire state of global cybersecurity and increasing reliance on centralization, as always, there’re vast areas that small teams can now disrupt that I’m excited to invest in.

quotedPost.author: mattpocockuk
quotedPost.text:
My hot take from chatting to @poteto is that we should use MORE abstractions in the AI age

You can use them (combined with harsh lint rules) to reduce the design space available to the agent and constrain them only to good decisions.

Combined with the fact that high-leverage abstractions let you do more with less code - so, more token efficient.

Plus, unwinding the damage from a bad abstraction is much cheaper with agents.

This runs counter to a lot of folks thinking that agents just want to read the raw code. They can, but they're not maximally efficient that way.

Be braver! Design abstractions.

records.author: antirez
records.text: So I'm thankful I was thinking like that. And I believe many other systems and companies that failed in between, all considered, now would not blindly buy the "lineraizable at all the costs" argument anymore.

records.author: antirez
records.text: So a system that takes some care to avoid common failure modes, or that just limits the outcome of failures, if it pays this compromise to have stellar properties when things don't go bad, it is a system that has a place.

records.author: antirez
records.text: Back in the days I realized that a system can't be characterized just for the way it handles whatever complex failure modes can be simulated, but it is actually the sum of how it behaves across all its lifetime of execution.

records.author: antirez
records.text: That's not to say that linearizability is not a good property for certain use cases, but that safety is actually a tradeoff, and one can be still vulnerabile to complex partitions/restarts scenarios while still having different degrees of real-world safety for most setups.

records.author: antirez
records.text: But I believe that not following the vision that wanted, in the late 2000s, every database to be able to guarantee strong consistency properties, was one of my best views that basically *saved* Redis from the same fate of many other systems that failed.

records.text: @Heliocene The use case is classification a  lot more than "decision".  Cambridge definition: A decision is a choice or conclusion you make AFTER THINKING about different possibilities

records.author: antirez
records.text: Calling classifiers "decision models" is a crime against machine learning. Those models decide *less* than LLMs, as you can think the CoT as a form of serial processing of information that such classifiers lack. Those models can be either *small* LLMs that are not let think, but instead the logits at the last position of the prefill are used to categorize in classes or, when they are BERT-alike, they compress the input meaning and project a class: in both cases they decide a lot less than an LLM.

records.author: poteto
records.text:
deleting the product
it's funny how you can sometimes tell if a team culture is dysfunctional just by looking at how their app is laid out. behind every feature, or tab in a sidebar likely lies a PM or someone responsible for an OKR.

the problem is when individual performance is measured by these metrics. it becomes the singular focus of the responsible person to make those numbers look good, since it determines whether they get rewarded or axed, even if it comes at the detriment of the overall quality of the product. this is why you mostly see features get added, but rarely removed. if you own a feature, then it being removed feels like an aura loss.

this is even worse in the agentic era when the cost to add features has become so low. you can simply will a new feature into existence overnight and add another tab. but users will notice that you ship your org chart.

teams that make people play silly games under the guise of performance management rarely build great products.

to build a great product you need to first fix your culture

Off the track, DHH:

Things included in this PR:

- Pi support.
- Auto-resume when limits reset
- T3 Code MCP (create, launch, message, wait on, read, search and interrupt threads)
- `delegate_task` lets an agent start child agents on any provider or model
- ACP Registry: add any registry agent (Devin, Cline, Kimi, Droid, and more)
- Cursor runs on the official Cursor SDK, not the (broken) CLI
- OpenCode 2 support
- Agents can rename threads, regenerate titles, link PRs and settle threads
- New MCP tools for worktree handoff, and for listing and closing previews
- Proper server-side queueing and steering
- Thread forking
- Switch provider or model in the middle of a thread
- Native subagents show as child threads in a lineage view, with their model, status and history
- Use `@` with a thread name, or drag a thread from the sidebar, to attach it as context
- Scheduled tasks
- Tons more I'm forgetting

Pumped this landed. We'll have a lot of cleanup to do to get it perfect, so expect lots of updates throughout the next few days :)

records.author: dwarkesh_sp
records.text:
New episode with military historian Si Sheppard.

The conquests of the Aztec and Inca empires might be the most shocking events in human history.

Hernan Cortés and some hundreds of Conquistadors landed on a new continent they knew basically nothing about, and within 2 and a half years, conquered the 6 million strong Aztec empire.

Then, a decade later, Francisco Pizarro did the same thing to an Incan Empire of some 10 million inhabitants.

In both cases, the Conquistadors consistently beat native armies while being literally 100x (or even in some cases 1000x) outnumbered - and in many cases, did so without taking a single casualty.

And they did this with 99% of their military forces being made up of the very natives they were trying to subjugate.

We often forget how wild human history is. People talk about AI takeover as if it would be some crazy, unprecedented sci-fi outcome. But this would not be the first time an alien force whose motives the defenders barely understand use more advanced technology and diplomatic cunning to outmaneuver and then take over a much larger and long established existing order.

0:00:00 – Cortés’s conquest of the Aztecs
0:22:39 – Pizarro’s conquest of the Inca
0:26:59 – Explaining Conquistador military superiority
0:34:39 – Could the natives have beat the Conquistadors?
0:48:56 – The Aztecs and Incas did not learn from each other
0:56:11 – Why Spain still lost in the long run
1:07:47 – Why didn’t the Aztecs/Incas adapt better to European warfare?
1:14:16 – Conquistador motivation
1:26:22 – Why Mughal India also couldn't play the Europeans off each other
1:33:42 – Diplomacy was just as important as technology

records.author: rauchg
records.text:
Most token aggregators have extreme noise from ① token promos from/to providers that train on your data or ② providers that *claim* to be ZDR.

Vercel AI Gateway is the largest trustworthy datasource to understand global AI token flows, because we have real usage, from real customers, an at-scale platform (400k+ paying customers and thousands of enterprises), and zero markup.

Notably… every week we turn down "free token" promos from companies that come to us with dubious claims of Zero Data Retention (ZDR) and questionable reputations. We also don't get a kick out of having the "most providers". Most providers suck. You want the *best* providers.

We put in as much work in engineering our gateway, as in our legal, compliance, privacy, and backoffice operations to responsibly serve trillions of tokens every day. We're here for the long haul.
